schools.summary: Calvin weighs the title Sheminith as a musical instrument or a tune, preferring the air to which the psalm was sung; Gill reads the godly man (chasid) as one beneficent, kind, and merciful, ceasing when reduced by death or by seeming-godly proving otherwise.
Clarke records the Arabic title (the eighth day, a prophecy of the Messiah's advent) and dates the psalm to the Babylonish captivity.
Augustine takes 'the eighth' mystically — the day of judgment, or the eternal age given the saints beyond the seven-day cycle of time.

Keil and Delitzsch parse hoshiah, gamar ('to have an end,' Ps. 7:9), the hapax pasas, chasid and amun ('one who is firm'); Ellicott holds 'the faithful' concrete against the Vulgate/Syriac abstract, cognate with 'amen' (Luther's 'amen's leute').

Henry makes it a psalm for bad times, the godly and faithful 'fast men' failing by death or desertion, as Elijah thought himself alone (Rom. 11:3); Spurgeon calls 'Help, Lord' an angel's sword, the godly's decline a trumpet-call to prayer.

sides.position: a musical instrument or a tune to which the psalm was set
'the eighth' taken mystically — the day of judgment or the eternal age
the eighth day / a Messianic title (the Arabic superscription)

debates.question: Is 'the faithful' (amunim) an abstract or a concrete?

sides.position: a concrete — faithful men, as good as their word

outliers.note: Reads the title's 'eighth' allegorically and eschatologically — the day of judgment or the eternal age of the saints — rather than as a musical or historical term.

schools.summary: Gill reads the vanity as doctrinal or practical falsehood, vain and corrupt, done in common as a token of the general degeneracy.
Clarke hears false, hollow men who say one thing and mean another; 'beleb valeb,' a heart and a heart, two hearts to flatter and to plot.
Henry sees dissimulation and flattery, men who 'kiss and kill' as Joab did Abner and Amasa — the devil's image complete, till an honest man knows not whom to trust.
Ellicott: 'vanity' literally 'evil'; 'lips of smoothness' (Ps. 5:9); 'a heart and a heart' (1 Chron. 12:33); possibly in Paul's mind (Eph. 4:25); Thomas Adams's 'a man with two hearts is a monster.'
Gill notes the clause may be prophecy or prayer (Aben Ezra, Kimchi); God cuts off the deceitful by judgment or everlasting punishment, death 'out of the world' (Targum) or hell.
Ellicott translates 'may Jehovah cut off,' 'proud things' = 'great things' (linguam magniloquam); Keil and Delitzsch read a true voluntative, 'may He root out' (Ps. 109:15; opp. Ps. 11:6).
Clarke takes 'proud things' (gedoloth) for the great swelling words used in promises and commendations.
Spurgeon: total destruction on flattery and pride ('raging waves foaming out their own shame'); the two sins are one vice, flattering another and flattering oneself, a lie in the right hand.

debates.question: Is 'the LORD shall cut off all flattering lips' a prophecy or a prayer?

sides.position: prophecy or prayer indifferently — it may be read either way
definitely a petition (the voluntative 'may He cut off / root out')

schools.summary: Gill reads 'with our tongue will we prevail' of men confident by eloquence or force; turns it to antichrist, 'we will make one to prevail,' the man of sin.
Clarke: 'our lips are our own,' men thinking speech gives licence; Wesley: prevailing by spreading evil reports, lips at their own disposal, none to control them.

Ellicott hears the boast of those with the ear of authority (Angelo defying Isabel), the rendering disputed ('masters of our tongues' / 'our tongues confederate'); Keil and Delitzsch weigh higbir, preferring 'we will give emphasis to our tongue,' lips as confederates.
Henry: the pride of men who fancy themselves as gods; 'our lips are our own' an unjust pretension (who made man's mouth?); 'who is lord over us?' the language of Pharaoh (Exod. 5:1).

debates.question: How is the boast 'with our tongue will we prevail' to be rendered?

sides.position: 'with our tongue will we prevail' — by our speech (AV)
'our tongues are our allies / we confederate,' or 'we give emphasis to our tongue'

themes: with our tongue will we prevail

schools.summary: Gill takes the oppressed poor for God's afflicted people, poor in estate and spirit, trodden down as Israel by Egypt.

Clarke refers the oppression to the captive Israelites in Babylon, 'now will I arise,' God alone their deliverer; Wesley reads 'puffeth at him' of the oppressor who despises and would destroy with a puff of breath.

Ellicott marks an ancient oracle quoted here, 'I will set in safety him that panteth for it' (Hab. 2:3); Keil and Delitzsch fix 'now' as the turn from forbearance to judgment (Isa. 33:10), rejecting 'him whom the boaster blows upon' for 'him who longs for' deliverance.
Spurgeon finds the oppression of the saints itself a cry that moves God as a father — Moses heard silent at the Red Sea — the needy set on high above the tormentor's rage.

debates.question: Does 'him that puffeth at him' name the oppressor's scorn or the sufferer's longing?

sides.position: the proud oppressor who blows upon / despises his victim
the poor man who pants and longs for the promised deliverance (Hab. 2:3)

schools.summary: Gill hears the words of God pure and holy against the wicked's deceit — Scriptures, promises, Gospel, the very Scriptures of truth.
Spurgeon: man's words yea and nay, God's yea and amen; the Bible through the furnace of persecution, criticism, doubt, and science has lost only its human alloy.

Clarke expounds the cupel — silver mingled with lead in calcined bone, purified till it lies still, the 'seven times' a perfect purification; Wesley: pure, without the least mixture of falsehood, infallibly fulfilled.

Ellicott labours over 'of earth' (ashes, or purified of the alloy) and reports Hitzig's emendation rats, 'a bar from the crucible' (Ps. 68:30); Keil and Delitzsch hear in the pure words the ground of the psalm's consolatory hope.

debates.question: What does 'a furnace of earth' mean?

sides.position: 'in earth' (the ashes the silver falls into) or 'as to earth' (purified of the alloy)
an emended text, rats — 'melted into a bar from the crucible'

themes: the words of the LORD are pure

schools.summary: Gill argues from the masculine affix that not the words (Aben Ezra) but the poor and needy are kept (Kimchi), preserved by God's power and in his Son from a final falling away.
Keil and Delitzsch read the suffixes of the miserable and poor and of the 'him' who yearned for deliverance, preserved so constantly that he will never succumb to this generation.
Wesley reads 'them' of God's words or promises, kept for ever; Clarke notes the variant 'us' (LXX, Vulgate, Arabic) and the historical keeping of Israel brought from Babylon.

debates.question: Whom or what does God 'preserve' — the words or the poor?

sides.position: the poor and needy people just set in safety
the words / promises of God just called pure

outliers.note: Brings a textual variant — several MSS with the Septuagint, Vulgate, and Arabic read 'us' for 'them' — and reads the preserving historically of Israel kept and brought out of Babylon.

schools.summary: Gill reads the wicked walking on every side of the righteous to watch and snare them, the whole world lying in wickedness.

Henry: vile men exalted to power protect vice, the wicked swarming as Sodom — when the wicked bear rule the people mourn; Spurgeon: vile rulers breed vice as sun breeds flies, yet the exalted Redeemer emboldens the saints, 'Help, Lord.'
Clarke renders 'as villany gains ground among the sons of Adam' (the Vulgate's turn); Wesley: the wicked fill all places and go about boldly and securely.

Ellicott reports Gesenius's 'like the rising of a tempest upon the sons of men' and offers 'the wicked vanish on every side' (Ps. 39:6); Keil and Delitzsch keep the plain 'when the vilest men are exalted.'

debates.question: How is the closing line 'when the vilest men are exalted' to be read?

sides.position: of vile men lifted into office (AV)
of vileness / villany spreading through the race (Vulgate)
of the wicked swept off like a rising tempest

themes: the wicked walk on every side
